title: Query Optimizer
description: Understand cost-based optimization, join ordering via dynamic programming, statistics with histograms and HyperLogLog, plan caching, and adaptive query execution.

segments.text: The query optimizer transforms a SQL query into an execution plan. For a simple three-table join, there are six possible join orderings. For ten tables, over three million. The optimizer must evaluate plans and find one with low cost in milliseconds. PostgreSQL's optimizer considers hundreds of alternative plans for complex queries. This is where database performance is won or lost.

Cost-based optimization estimates the cost of each plan using statistics about the data. Cost equals CPU cost plus I/O cost. A full table scan on a million-row table: one million page reads. An index scan returning one hundred rows: one hundred random I/O operations. The optimizer chooses the plan with the lowest estimated total cost.

Join ordering uses dynamic programming. For N tables, build optimal plans bottom-up: first find the best way to join each pair, then each triple using the best pairs, and so on. PostgreSQL uses this for up to twelve tables. Beyond twelve, it switches to a genetic algorithm — GEQO — because dynamic programming becomes too expensive.

Statistics drive optimizer accuracy. Histograms capture value distribution — is the data uniform or skewed? HyperLogLog estimates distinct value count using only kilobytes of memory — essential for cardinality estimation. If the optimizer thinks a filter returns ten rows but it actually returns ten million, it picks the wrong plan. Stale statistics are the number one cause of bad query plans.

Your query joins three tables. The optimizer estimates the join produces one thousand rows and chooses a nested loop join. In reality, it produces ten million rows. The query takes three hours instead of three seconds. How do you diagnose and fix this?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you diagnose a query plan with wildly wrong cardinality estimates? What tools and fixes?

segments.text: Plan caching avoids re-optimizing the same query repeatedly. PostgreSQL caches plans for prepared statements after five executions. But cached plans can become stale when data distribution changes. The solution: invalidate cached plans when statistics are updated or when the estimated and actual row counts diverge significantly — adaptive plan invalidation.

Adaptive query execution — used by Spark AQE and Oracle — adjusts the plan at runtime. After processing the first stage, check actual row counts. If they differ significantly from estimates, re-optimize remaining stages. Spark AQE can switch from sort-merge join to broadcast hash join mid-query when it discovers one side is small enough.

Three join algorithms, each optimal for different data sizes. Nested loop join: O(N times M), best when one side is tiny. Hash join: O(N plus M), best for large equi-joins when hash table fits in memory. Sort-merge join: O(N log N plus M log M), best when data is already sorted or when result needs ordering. The optimizer picks based on estimated cardinality.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE is your X-ray into the optimizer's decisions. It shows the chosen plan, estimated vs actual row counts, and time per operation. Look for: sequential scans on large tables where index scans should be used, nested loops on large cardinalities, and large differences between estimated and actual rows — these indicate statistics problems.
You're building a query optimizer for a distributed database. Queries span multiple nodes. How does distribution change the cost model? What new costs must you consider beyond CPU and I/O?
segments.thought_prompt: How does distributed execution change query optimization? What costs are unique to distributed queries?

segments.text: Query optimization is cost-based search through the plan space. Dynamic programming finds optimal join orders, statistics drive cardinality estimates, plan caching amortizes optimization cost, and adaptive execution corrects mistakes at runtime. The Staff-level insight: understanding the optimizer is understanding why your query is slow — it's almost always a statistics problem.
